title: Winner-take-all_in_action_selection
summary:
Winner-take-all is a computer science concept that has been widely applied in behavior-based robotics as a method of action selection for intelligent agents. Winner-take-all systems work by connecting modules (task-designated areas) in such a way that when one action is performed it stops all other actions from being performed, so only one action is occurring at a time. The name comes from the idea that the "winner" action takes all of the motor system's power.

In the 1980s and 1990s, many roboticists and cognitive scientists were attempting to find speedier alternatives to traditional world modeling. In 1982, Jerome A. Feldman and D.H. Ballard published "Connectionist Models and Their Properties," referencing winner-take-all as a method of action selection. In 1986, Rodney Brooks introduced behavior-based artificial intelligence. Winner-take-all architectures for action selection soon became a common feature of behavior-based robots, because selection occurred at the level of the action modules (bottom-up) rather than at a separate cognitive level (top-down), producing a tight coupling of stimulus and reaction.

Three main architectures exist. Hierarchical: actions are programmed in a high-to-low priority list with inhibitory connections; the agent performs low-priority behaviors until a higher-priority behavior is stimulated, at which point it inhibits all others. Arbiter/Centrally Coordinated: action modules are connected to a central arbiter; when behaviors are triggered, they send votes to the arbiter, and the behavior with the highest number of votes is selected, with bias created through voting weight. Heterarchy/Fully Distributed: each behavior has pre-conditions and post-conditions determining behavior order; modules can receive input from other modules as well as sensors, so modules can recruit each other.

In neural networks, winner-take-all is a computational principle by which neurons compete with each other for activation. In the classical form, only the neuron with the highest activation stays active while all other neurons shut down. Winner-take-all networks are commonly used in computational models of the brain for distributed decision-making or action selection in the cortex, and are also common in artificial neural networks and neuromorphic analog VLSI circuits.
